turns.transcript: Hey Mellow, something really strange just happened. I used an LLM to tidy up my essay, and now it sounds almost identical to my friend's writing. Same tone, same structure—even some of the examples are eerily similar. Do you have any idea what’s going on here?

What you're experiencing lines up with a known effect. There’s a recent paper called “How LLMs Distort Our Written Language” by Abdulhai and others, published just a few days ago. They found that heavy reliance on LLMs can strip away personal voice and make different pieces of writing converge toward a single, neutral style. So, your essay and your friend’s might have been pulled in the same direction by the LLM.

Wow, that’s really fascinating—and a bit unsettling. I didn’t realize those tools could actually flatten out our individual voices like that. How did they actually measure that voice loss? What metrics did they use, and what did the data look like?

They used something called sentence embeddings to measure the similarity between different pieces of writing. Essentially, they turned each essay into a vector in a high-dimensional space and then looked at how close those vectors ended up after LLM revisions. What they found was that all the essays started to cluster around one point, indicating that the individual “voice” of each writer was getting lost. On top of that, they used linguistic analysis tools to track changes in emotional, analytic, and structural language. They found big shifts even when the LLM only made small grammar tweaks. So it’s both subtle and widespread.

That’s honestly mind-blowing. The idea that even tiny grammar edits could push everything toward some standard style is wild. But now I’m wondering—if something as simple as grammar corrections can do that, what about scientific peer review or other expert edits? Are we all just heading toward the same uniform way of writing?

That’s exactly what the paper dives into. They found the same flattening effect in scientific peer reviews. When reviews were AI-generated or heavily edited by LLMs, they tended to place less emphasis on the unique significance or clarity of the research. Instead, everything trended toward a more neutral and generic tone. So yes, there’s a real risk that expert domains could lose their diversity of perspective and style. That’s why the paper suggests using LLMs more for information retrieval, rather than writing your text. It's a way to preserve your own voice and perspective.

Thanks so much, Mellow. This has been a huge eye-opener. I never realized how subtle but widespread this effect could be. I’ll definitely rethink how I use these tools moving forward. It’s so important to keep our individuality. Thanks again for the insight—it’s been amazing chatting with you. I guess one last thing I’ll be thinking about now is what it means for all of us if we start sounding the same. Thanks again, and take care!

You’re very welcome! It’s been wonderful talking with you about this. You’ve really grasped the core point—individual voice matters, and these tools can subtly push us toward uniformity. You’ve got a great instinct for recognizing when something feels off, and that’s so valuable. Keep trusting that instinct, and use these tools in ways that support your unique voice, not replace it. Take care, and keep shining with your own style!
